1:
TEACHER NOTES:
This title slide opens Lesson 7. Have pencil, mini whiteboards, textas and booklets out before you click off this slide.
2:
TEACHER NOTES:
Planning slide for the teacher. The Extended Path is the 60 minute version. Use the full deck unless your time slot is shorter.
3:
TEACHER NOTES:
Pre-read the matching Teacher Handbook before teaching. The shared text on slides 10 to 15 is Shearing Sheep, an informative text about wool and shearing. Decide your pause points and any incidental vocabulary in advance.
4:
TEACHER NOTES:
Quick icon reference. I = I do, W = We do, CfU = Check for understanding, Y = You do. Skip past for students.
5:
TEACHER NOTES:
Legend for student response routines used through the deck. Whiteboard response, choral response, thumbs and show fingers come up most often.
6:
TEACHER NOTES:
Icon legend only. No teaching action required.
7:
TEACHER NOTES:
Reference chart for the colour coded sentence parts. Use only if you plan to colour code parts of speech today.
8:
SAY:
- "We need three things on our desks."
- "Pencil. Mini whiteboard with a texta. Booklet."
- "Show me your texta up high when you are ready."

DO:
- Point to each item on the slide as students get it out.
- Wait until every student has all three before moving on.

TEACHER NOTES:
Quick set up slide. Do not start the read aloud until every student has a working board and texta.

WATCH FOR:
- Students with no texta or a dry texta. Top up before reading begins.
9:
TEACHER NOTES:
Divider for the shared read aloud of Shearing Sheep. Use it to settle the class. Eyes up before slide 10.
10:
SAY:
- "Listen. We are reading a true text called Shearing Sheep."
- "Read with me. Sheep grow thick, woolly coats called fleeces."
- "Just like people get haircuts, sheep need their wool cut too."
- "Ask: what is shearing? Expected: when the sheep's wool is cut off."
- "Ask: how often does it happen? Expected: about once a year."

DO:
- Point to the photo on the slide.
- Read the paragraph aloud at a steady pace.
- Pause after the word "shearing" and tap it.

TEACHER NOTES:
First paragraph of the informative text. Anchor the new word "shearing" before moving on. The image is the visual anchor for what a fleece looks like.

WATCH FOR:
- Students confusing shearing with sharing. Quick correction: shearing is cutting the wool.
11:
SAY:
- "Read with me. The person who cuts the wool is called a shearer."
- "Shearers need a lot of skill. They use special clippers."
- "Ask: how long does it take to shear one sheep? Expected: just a few minutes."
- "Ask: where does the wool go next? Expected: thrown on a table to be cleaned and rolled, then pressed into bales."

DO:
- Point to the picture of the shearer at work.
- Tap the word shearer when you say it. Compare it to shearing.
- Show the rolling and packing steps with a hand gesture if you like.

TEACHER NOTES:
Introduces the role of the shearer and the journey of the wool. The vocabulary word "skill" appears here and is taught fully on slide 17.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who lose track of the steps. Recap with three fingers: cut, clean and roll, pack into bales.
12:
SAY:
- "Read with me. Shearing mostly happens in spring or summer."
- "Ask: why then? Expected: because it is warmer and the sheep do not need their heavy coats."
- "Without shearing, sheep would be too hot."

DO:
- Point to the photo. Ask students to notice the warm weather signs.
- Use a hand fan gesture for hot.

TEACHER NOTES:
Links shearing to the seasons. Keep students focused on cause and effect: warm weather, no heavy coat needed.

WATCH FOR:
- Students naming the season but not the reason. Prompt: "Why spring or summer?"
13:
SAY:
- "Read with me. Freshly shorn sheep often look small and skinny, but they feel much better."
- "Ask: why is shearing important for sheep health? Expected: long fleeces trap dirt and bugs, which can make the sheep sick."

DO:
- Point to the photo of the shorn sheep on the slide.
- Read both parts of the paragraph clearly.
- Tap the words clean and healthy when you say them.

TEACHER NOTES:
Key idea: shearing keeps sheep healthy and clean. Build the cause to effect chain: long fleece -> dirt and bugs -> sickness.

WATCH FOR:
- Students focused only on how the sheep looks. Prompt: "What about how the sheep feels?"
14:
SAY:
- "Read with me. Australia and New Zealand have huge shearing sheds."
- "Ask: how many sheep can be shorn in a day? Expected: hundreds."
- "Ask: who travels around at shearing time? Expected: shearers, helpers and cooks."

DO:
- Point to both photos.
- Show the size of a shearing shed with two open arms.

TEACHER NOTES:
New information about scale and teams. The two countries named are Australia and New Zealand. Some shearers compete to be the fastest.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who cannot recall both countries. Recap: Australia and New Zealand.
15:
SAY:
- "Read with me. Good shearers work quickly and gently."
- "The wool the sheep leave behind is made into clothing."
- "Ask: what kinds of clothing? Expected: jumpers, scarves and blankets, which keep people warm."

DO:
- Point to each picture as you read.
- Hold up your jumper sleeve and link it back to the sheep.

TEACHER NOTES:
Final paragraph closes the loop from sheep to clothing. Use this to recap the whole journey before vocabulary work.

WATCH FOR:
- Students naming only one item. Prompt: "What else can wool be made into?"
16:
TEACHER NOTES:
Divider for the vocabulary section. Two words are taught: skill and remove. Boards stay out for the show me responses.
17:
SOURCES:
Definition adapted from Collins Primary School Dictionary, accessed 30.10.25.

SAY:
- "Watch this first."
- "In the text we read that shearers have a lot of skill to remove the fleece."
- "Skill is the knowledge and ability that lets you do something well."
- "Say the word with me: skill."
- "Playing a musical instrument or doing a gymnastics routine takes skill."

DO:
- Point to each numbered photo and name what skill is shown.
- Tap the definition card as you read it.
- Cue choral response: "Say it with me: skill."

TEACHER NOTES:
First vocabulary slide. Anchor the meaning to the photos before students use the word in slide 18.

WATCH FOR:
- Students saying the word but not the meaning. Prompt: "What does skill mean?"
18:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers."
- "In the text Shearing Sheep, who needs a lot of skill?"
- "Ask: 1 for the sheep, 2 for the shearer."

DO:
- Wait. Boards down, fingers up.
- Reveal the shearer is the answer.
- Tap the word skill and the photo of the shearer.

TEACHER NOTES:
Links the new word back to the read aloud. Quick check that students can apply the word to the right person.

WATCH FOR:
- Students choosing the sheep. Quick correction: the shearer does the cutting and that takes skill.
19:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers."
- "If you are skilled at something, you are..."
- "Ask: 1 for good at it, 2 for still learning."

DO:
- Cue silent thinking, then fingers up.
- Reveal: good at it.
- Repeat the meaning: skill is doing something well.

TEACHER NOTES:
Quick definition check. Some students may say "still learning" because they are still learning at school. Reset to the word skilled.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick "still learning." Quick correction: "Skilled means already good at it."
20:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers."
- "Which pictures show someone using a skill?"
- "Pick all that show a skill."

DO:
- Read each option aloud: shooting a goal, riding a bike, sleeping.
- Take fingers up after a short think.
- Reveal: shooting a goal and riding a bike are skills. Sleeping is not.

TEACHER NOTES:
Good example and non-example slide. Sleeping is the non-example. Use it to show that a skill takes practice.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who choose sleeping. Quick correction: "Did we have to learn how to sleep? No. So sleeping is not a skill."
21:
SAY:
- "Turn and tell your partner."
- "What is a skill you would like to have? Why?"
- "Use the word skill or skilled in your answer."

DO:
- Read the two examples on the slide aloud.
- Give 30 to 45 seconds for partner talk.
- Take 2 to 3 student responses to share with the class.

TEACHER NOTES:
Use the example responses on the slide as models. Push students to use the new word in their reply.

WATCH FOR:
- Students naming a skill but not using the word. Prompt: "Use the word skill in your answer."
22:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers."
- "Which activity requires skill? Pick the one that takes practice."

DO:
- Wait silently while students choose.
- Cue fingers up at the same time.
- Confirm the correct activity by tapping the photo.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers
Script:
- Ask: which activity requires skill? Expected: the activity that takes practice and learning, not an everyday action.
- Scan for: most students pointing to the same option.
PROCEED:
- >=80% pick the practised activity. Move to the second word: remove.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students pick an option that does not need learning.
- Reteach: ask "Did you have to learn to do this? Did it take practice?"
- Re-check: ask "Is walking a skill? Why or why not?"

TEACHER NOTES:
Final check on skill before moving to the next word. Confirm the answer against the slide before teaching.

WATCH FOR:
- Students guessing fast. Use boards down, think, then show fingers.
23:
SOURCES:
Definition from Collins Primary School Dictionary, accessed 31.10.25.

SAY:
- "Watch this first."
- "In the text we read that shearers can remove the fleece in just a few minutes."
- "Remove means to take something away."
- "Say the word with me: remove."
- "You might remove a lid from a jar, or remove your shoes at the door."

DO:
- Mime taking off a lid as you say remove.
- Point to each photo on the slide.
- Cue choral response: "Remove."

TEACHER NOTES:
Second vocabulary word. Anchor the meaning with the lid and shoe examples before students apply it in slide 24.

WATCH FOR:
- Students copying the word but not the meaning. Prompt: "What does remove mean? Take something away."
24:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers."
- "Which sheep has had its fleece removed?"
- "Look at both pictures carefully."

DO:
- Wait. Fingers up.
- Reveal the shorn sheep. Tap the word removed.

TEACHER NOTES:
Links remove back to the text. The shorn sheep looks small and pink because the wool has been taken away.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who choose the woolly sheep. Quick correction: "Has the wool been taken away here?"
25:
SAY:
- "Three questions. Show me thumbs up for yes, thumbs down for no."
- "Would you remove a pencil line with an eraser? Yes."
- "Would you remove your beanie if you were hot? Yes."
- "Would you remove a door to go inside? No, you open the door."

DO:
- Read each option, pause, and watch thumbs.
- Reveal each answer in turn.

TEACHER NOTES:
Three quick yes or no checks. The non-example is removing a door, since that is not what we usually do.

WATCH FOR:
- Students putting thumbs up for the door. Quick correction: "Do we take a door away to go inside? No, we open it."
26:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers."
- "In which activities would you remove something? Pick all that fit."
- "Planting a tree, picking flowers, weeding."

DO:
- Read each option aloud.
- Take fingers up at the same time.
- Reveal: picking flowers and weeding involve removing. Planting a tree adds something instead.

TEACHER NOTES:
Good example and non-example sort. Planting is the non-example because you are putting something in, not taking it away.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick planting a tree. Quick correction: "Do we take something away when we plant? No, we put it in."
27:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers."
- "Which words mean nearly the same as remove?"
- "Take away. Get rid of. Build."

DO:
- Read each option aloud.
- Reveal: take away and get rid of mean nearly the same as remove. Build is the opposite.

TEACHER NOTES:
Simple synonym sort. Build is the trap because it is the opposite of removing.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick build. Quick correction: "To build is to make. The opposite of remove."
28:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers."
- "Which child has been able to remove their shoes?"

DO:
- Wait. Fingers up.
- Reveal the photo of the child with no shoes.
- Tap the word remove.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers
Script:
- Ask: which child has been able to remove their shoes? Expected: the child whose shoes are off.
- Scan for: most students pointing to the matching number.
PROCEED:
- >=80% correct. Move to the writing focus on slide 29.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students miss that the shoes need to be already off, not just untied.
- Reteach: "Remove means to take away. The shoes have been taken off."
- Re-check: ask "What other things could you remove from yourself? Hat? Backpack?"

TEACHER NOTES:
Final vocabulary check before moving into editing. Confirm both new words have stuck.

WATCH FOR:
- Students choosing the child with shoes still on. Quick correction: "Have the shoes been taken away?"
29:
TEACHER NOTES:
Divider for the editing focus. Reset the room: book away, boards out, eyes up. Move to slide 30 once everyone is ready.
30:
SAY:
- "Watch and listen first."
- "Editing means checking a sentence carefully so it is correct."
- "Good writers always edit."
- "There are three things to look for. A capital letter at the start. Capital letters for proper nouns. Punctuation at the end."

DO:
- Point to each line of the checklist as you say it.
- Tap your three fingers to count: start, names, end.
- Keep boards down. Students watch.

TEACHER NOTES:
This is the editing checklist that returns on every We Do slide in this section. Make sure students can recall the three checks before moving on.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who can repeat the words but not the actions. Prompt one student to point to a capital letter at the start of any nearby sentence.
31:
SAY:
- "Watch this first."
- "Read with me: jess fed vanessa and the chicks in october."
- "Find the nouns. The names are Jess, Vanessa and October."
- "Chicks is a common noun, the general name for that animal."
- "Now I add capitals on the proper nouns and on the start of the sentence."
- "Then I add the full stop at the end."

DO:
- Read the lowercase sentence aloud first.
- Tap each proper noun as you change it.
- Reveal the corrected sentence: Jess fed Vanessa and the chicks in October.

TEACHER NOTES:
First worked example for editing. The teacher does the thinking out loud. The visible checklist on the slide is the anchor.

WATCH FOR:
- Students wanting to capitalise chicks. Quick reminder: chicks is the type, not the name.
32:
SAY:
- "Read with me: Jess fed Vanessa and the chicks in October."
- "Now I check using the editing list."
- "Capital at the start? Yes, the J on Jess."
- "Capitals for proper nouns? Yes, Jess, Vanessa and October."
- "Punctuation at the end? Yes, full stop."

DO:
- Read each item in the checklist and tap the matching part of the sentence.
- Add the full stop on screen if it is not yet there.
- Reveal the final sentence: Jess fed Vanessa and the chicks in October.

TEACHER NOTES:
This is the explicit modelling of using the checklist. Show that a sentence can pass all three checks at once.

WATCH FOR:
- Students rushing past the start of sentence check. Slow them down to do all three checks every time.
33:
SAY:
- "Read with me: look at maria chasing georgie across the yard."
- "On your board, find the nouns. Show me the proper nouns."
- "Ask: which words need capital letters? Expected: Maria and Georgie."
- "What punctuation goes at the end? It is telling us something. Full stop."

DO:
- Read the lowercase sentence first.
- Wait while students write or underline.
- Reveal the changes one step at a time: Maria, Georgie, capital L, full stop.

TEACHER NOTES:
First guided practice. Two proper nouns plus the start and end. Use the checklist on screen as the anchor.

WATCH FOR:
- Students missing the capital L at the start. Use the checklist: "Capital at the start?"
34:
SAY:
- "Read with me: we hope mum and dad will get us a pony for christmas."
- "On your board, edit this sentence using the checklist."
- "Mum and Dad are used as names here, so they are proper nouns."
- "Show me your sentence."

DO:
- Read the lowercase sentence aloud.
- Wait silently while students write.
- Reveal the edits step by step: Mum, Dad, Christmas, capital W on We, full stop.

TEACHER NOTES:
Three special name words to capitalise: Mum, Dad, Christmas. Plus the start and end. Christmas is one specific day, so it is a proper noun.

WATCH FOR:
- Students leaving Christmas in lowercase. Quick reminder: special days have capitals, just like months.
35:
SAY:
- "Turn to page 6 of the text."
- "Look at the picture. What is Maria the cat doing?"
- "Read with me: maria is trying to catch a parrot, so we put her in the shed with tiger."
- "On your board, edit the sentence. Use the checklist."

DO:
- Hold the book open at page 6 so students can see Maria.
- Wait while students edit.
- Reveal Maria, Tiger, capital M at the start, full stop at the end.

TEACHER NOTES:
Links the editing back to the text on page 6. Maria and Tiger are the proper nouns. Parrot stays lowercase because it is a type, not a name.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who capitalise parrot or shed. Quick correction: "Is parrot a name or a type? Type, so no capital."
36:
SAY:
- "Read with me: yesterday maria and little tom were climbing tall trees."
- "Edit the sentence on your board."
- "Special note: Little Tom is the kitten's name, so both words have capitals."

DO:
- Read the sentence aloud first.
- Pause for 60 seconds while students write.
- Reveal Maria, Little Tom, capital Y at the start, full stop.

TEACHER NOTES:
The trickier piece on this slide is that both words of Little Tom take a capital because the whole name belongs to one specific kitten.

WATCH FOR:
- Students leaving little in lowercase. Quick reminder: when little is part of the name, it gets a capital.
37:
SAY:
- "Watch this first."
- "Most sentences end with a full stop."
- "A question ends with a question mark."
- "A sentence with strong feeling ends with an exclamation mark."
- "Read with me: How many trees are you planting, Mum? That is a question, so question mark."
- "Read with me: Stop eating the apricots, Georgie! That has strong feeling, so exclamation mark."

DO:
- Point to each end mark on the slide as you read it.
- Use voice colour: rising voice for the question, urgent voice for the exclamation.

TEACHER NOTES:
Introduces question marks and exclamation marks. The full stop is still the most common, but students need to know when to swap.

WATCH FOR:
- Students using a question mark on a normal sentence. Quick reminder: only use ? when the sentence is asking something.
38:
SAY:
- "Read with me: can you teach me how to milk lillypilly please mum."
- "This sentence is asking something. What punctuation should we use at the end?"
- "Edit the sentence on your board. Show me when you are ready."

DO:
- Read the sentence with rising voice to flag the question.
- Wait for boards.
- Reveal: Lillypilly, Mum, capital C at the start, question mark at the end.

TEACHER NOTES:
This is a question sentence. The clue is "Can you teach me..." which is asking for something. Two proper nouns: Lillypilly and Mum.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who put a full stop at the end. Quick correction: "Is this asking something? Yes, so question mark."
39:
SAY:
- "Turn to page 25 of the text."
- "Look at the picture. What does the family notice about Daisy?"
- "Read with me: i can't believe how big daisy the lamb is now."
- "This is a sentence with strong feeling. What punctuation should we use at the end?"
- "Edit the sentence on your board."

DO:
- Hold the book open at page 25.
- Read the sentence with surprise in your voice.
- Reveal Daisy, capital I at the start, exclamation mark at the end.

TEACHER NOTES:
Links the editing back to page 25 of the text. The sentence is an exclamation because of the strong feeling.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who use a full stop. Quick correction: "Is this sentence said with strong feeling? Yes, so exclamation mark."
40:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers."
- "What are we looking for in the editing process today?"

DO:
- Read each option aloud once.
- Cue silent think, then fingers up.
- Reveal the correct option: capital letter to start the sentence, capital letters for proper nouns, punctuation at the end.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers
Script:
- Ask: what are we looking for when we edit a sentence? Expected: capital at the start, capitals for proper nouns, punctuation at the end.
- Scan for: most students choosing the option that matches the three checks.
PROCEED:
- >=80% pick the correct option. Move to slide 41.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students pick the option about adjectives, mixing up nouns and describing words.
- Reteach: tap the editing checklist on screen and read each item again.
- Re-check: ask "What is the third thing we check?"

TEACHER NOTES:
Quick recall check on the editing checklist. If most students miss this, reteach the three checks before moving to the booklet task.

WATCH FOR:
- Students choosing the answer with adjectives. Quick correction: adjectives describe a noun, but they are not part of the editing checklist.
41:
SAY:
- "Show me on your fingers."
- "Which sentence is correctly punctuated?"
- "Look at the start, the proper nouns and the end."

DO:
- Wait silently. Boards down.
- Cue fingers up.
- Reveal: Lillypilly and her calf Billy eat grass.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers
Script:
- Ask: which sentence is correctly punctuated? Expected: Lillypilly and her calf Billy eat grass.
- Scan for: most students pointing to the same number.
PROCEED:
- >=80% correct. Move to the booklet task on slide 42.
PIVOT:
- Most likely: students pick a version with lowercase Lillypilly, lowercase Billy or no full stop.
- Reteach: read each option aloud and ask "Does it pass all three checks?"
- Re-check: write "the cat sleeps" on the board and ask "Does this pass all three checks?"

TEACHER NOTES:
Final check before independent work. Two proper nouns to capitalise: Lillypilly and Billy. Full stop at the end.

WATCH FOR:
- Students rushing without checking all three things. Slow them down with the checklist.
42:
SAY:
- "Open your booklet to Lesson 7: Sentence-level writing."
- "Eyes back here when your booklet is open and your pencil is out."

DO:
- Wait until every student has the right page.
- Read the page heading aloud once.

TEACHER NOTES:
Transition to the booklet task. Use this moment to settle the room before independent work.

WATCH FOR:
- Students still on the wrong page. Pause and reset before students start writing.
43:
TEACHER NOTES:
Acknowledgement and credits slide. No teaching action required.
